newsitem.title: ITALY: Suspended Italian army sergeant says he no torturer.
newsitem.headline: Suspended Italian army sergeant says he no torturer.

text.p: An Italian army sergeant suspended from duty amid an uproar about alleged human rights abuses by troops in Somalia said on Monday that he was not a torturer and that published photographs gave the wrong impression.
"What torture?" paratrooper Valerio Ercole, wearing uniform despite his suspension, asked a news conference he called at his lawyer's office in Rome.
"The real tortured ones are me and my family.
"I am a soldier and I carry a gun. You on the other hand carry pens. I never killed anyone in Somalia but you with your pens have tried, condemned and sentenced me already."

The news magazine Panorama has published photographs and allegations charging that Italian troops involved in a U.S.-led multinational mission to Somalia from 1992 to 1994 indulged in horrific abuses including sexual assault and killings.
The allegations, accompanied by interviews with Italian soldiers, have caused deep shock in Italy which has taken great pride in the role of its military in peacekeeping efforts.
"A myth has been shattered," Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta told the daily Corriere della Sera.

"Italians have always thought of their soldiers in this way: maybe not as efficient as those of other countries but capable of winning affection and operating in difficult circumstances, even in wars, without being domineering.
"It is a characteristic that the country has always been proud of. The brutality of the Somalia revelations has cast doubts over that notion," Andreatta said.
The allegations also coincide with Italian leadership of a multinational security force deployed in Albania, where elections are due to be held on June 29.
Generals Bruno Loi and Carmine Fiore, who led Italian forces in Somalia, resigned on Saturday saying their gesture demonstrated that the armed forces wanted the truth to be told.

A five-member commission, headed by respected judge Ettore Gallo who was himself tortured in World War Two by Nazi German SS forces, has been named by the government to head an urgent inquiry. It met for the first time on Monday.

The commission includes two generals and two women -- ex-minister Tina Anselmi, a former wartime partisan, and Tullia Zevi, head of Italy's Jewish Communities. The commission is expected to report back in a month.

Ercole admitted he was the man in one photograph published by Panorama two weeks ago which showed a soldier apparently about to affix what looked like electrodes to the genitals of a naked, prone Somali man.
He said the camera gave a false impression.
"They are not electrodes but just telephone wires, from a field telephone that would not hurt a fly," Ercole said.
Ercole said that Somali police had brought the man and two others to the Italians because they believed they had information about a large arms cache.
"They asked me to frighten him. Those wires were just a bluff, I didn't even touch him," he said.
"Maybe some people have already forgotten, but there was a war down there, we were not on a peacekeeping mission."
Other published photographs showed soldiers seemingly assaulting a semi-naked woman tied to an armoured car.
The scandal has prompted calls from some political parties, particularly on the left, for the disbanding of Italy's elite Folgore paratroop division, which served in Somalia.
Fatuma Hagi Yassin, leader of the Somali community in Italy, on Monday called for a meeting with Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro to discuss the situation.
